analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, raises penalties for safety violations, and expands miners' right to refuse dangerous work.
analysis.headline: The mine safety bill, introduced after the Upper Big Branch disaster that killed 29 miners, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal mine safety law and parts of the general workplace safety law. It would require independent investigations of major mine disasters, let miners talk to federal investigators without their boss's lawyers present, pay miners their full wages for the whole time they are idled by a safety shutdown, protect miners who refuse unsafe work, raise fines and prison terms for operators who knowingly violate safety rules, put repeat-offender mines under a strict pattern-of-violations regime, and require mines to install monitoring equipment that detects explosive gases and coal dust. It was referred to the Senate health committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, who get stronger protection from retaliation, full pay during safety shutdowns, more training, better dust and gas monitoring, and independent disaster investigations; their families, who can designate representatives in accidents; and workers generally, through new OSHA retaliation protections and victims' rights.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent investigation panel for any mine accident involving three or more deaths, in addition to the Labor Department's own investigation.
Lets any miner speak privately with federal investigators without the presence, involvement, or knowledge of the mine operator or its attorneys.
Entitles miners idled by a safety withdrawal order to full pay at their regular rate for the entire period, instead of the balance of their shift plus up to four hours under current law.
Protects miners from being fired or disciplined for refusing work they reasonably believe is dangerous, and raises the penalty for retaliation to $10,000-$100,000 per violation.

Raises criminal penalties for knowing safety violations that cause a death to fines up to $1,000,000 and up to 5 years in prison, and up to $2,000,000 and 10 years for repeat violations, and makes individual officers and directors personally liable for violations they authorize.

Creates a public, searchable database of every mine's safety records and places mines with recurring citations, accidents, or injuries into a pattern-of-violations status that brings withdrawal orders, more inspections, and operator-paid inspection fees.
Requires underground coal mines to install atmospheric monitoring systems and equipment-mounted devices that detect methane, carbon monoxide, oxygen, and coal dust levels in real time.

Amends the OSHA law to strengthen protections against retaliation, give workers victims' rights in enforcement proceedings, and increase civil and criminal penalties for employers whose violations kill or seriously injure employees.

analysis.who_pays: Mine operators, who would face higher fines, personal liability for executives, operator-funded inspections for repeat offenders, new monitoring equipment, stricter dust standards, and more training hours. Employers generally would face higher OSHA penalties and new victims' rights in enforcement cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose significant new costs on mine operators: civil penalties up to $150,000 per significant violation, doubled penalties for mines that miss performance benchmarks, fees to fund extra inspections, mandatory monitoring equipment, and a new 80 percent rock dust standard.

A mine placed in pattern status would be shut down entirely, with all workers withdrawn, until the operator meets strict performance benchmarks and the Secretary approves a remediation plan, which could idle an operation for a long period.

The Secretary would write the regulations that define pattern status and its benchmarks, and courts would have to defer to the Secretary's plan decisions unless a challenger shows they were arbitrary or capricious, concentrating considerable enforcement discretion in one agency.
Higher fixed compliance costs fall hardest on smaller operators and could accelerate mine closures, which would cost mining jobs in coal-dependent communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are concrete and life-or-death: miners killed in preventable explosions are the reason the bill exists, and its independent investigations, whistleblower protections, full pay during shutdowns, and monitoring technology all target the documented failures that killed 29 miners at Upper Big Branch. The costs are real but ordinary for safety regulation: more fines, fees, equipment, and shutdown risk for operators, with the heaviest burden on marginal mines. The bill's main design weakness is the amount of discretionary power it hands the Secretary of Labor, which defenders of operator rights reasonably flagged. On balance it is a worker-safety bill whose costs fall on the industry whose practices it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 25, 2012, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Rockefeller introduced the bill on July 25, 2012, joined by Senators Harkin, Murray, and Manchin.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken; the bill received no committee markup, no floor debate, and no vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

The bill's findings section documents the motivation: the April 2010 Upper Big Branch mine explosion in West Virginia killed 29 miners, and multiple investigations concluded it was a preventable explosion caused by the operator's failure to follow known safety standards.
The findings also note that investigators had made recommendations that could only be accomplished through legislation, and that Congress had not yet passed comprehensive mine safety legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mine operators came out ahead: they avoided higher fines, executive liability, pattern-status shutdowns, inspection fees, and new monitoring equipment requirements. The bill's supporters gained nothing, and no reform of mine safety law passed in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mine operators, who avoided new costs

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members stood; all four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill raises fines to $150,000 per significant violation, doubles penalties for repeat offenders, extends criminal exposure to executives personally, adds operator-paid inspection fees, and can shut down pattern-status mines entirely. The operators' cost is the safety gain for the roughly mine workforce exposed to those hazards.

industries.industry: Employers covered by OSHA (all regulated workplaces)
industries.note: Title VII raises OSHA civil penalties, adds criminal penalties for knowing violations that kill or seriously injure workers, and gives injured workers and victims' families rights in enforcement proceedings. The cost to employers of serious violations is the added protection for their employees.

The bill mandates atmospheric monitoring systems in underground coal mines and equipment-mounted devices that detect methane, carbon monoxide, oxygen, and coal dust, creating a mandated market for monitoring technology. The same equipment directly protects miners.
